India–US Relations Since 1947

India–US relations have evolved from Cold War-era differences and strategic distance into a broad-based strategic partnership covering defence, technology, trade, energy, space, critical minerals and the Indo-Pacific.

The Beginning: 1947–1962

India and the United States established diplomatic relations in 1946, even before India became independent.

After independence, India followed a policy of Non-Alignment, choosing not to formally join either the US-led or Soviet-led Cold War blocs.

The two countries nevertheless cooperated in:

• Economic and development assistance
• Food security and agriculture
• Education and scientific cooperation
• Economic and technical assistance

However, the United States developed close security ties with Pakistan, while India maintained increasingly close relations with the Soviet Union.

1962: India-China War
The 1962 India-China War created temporary strategic convergence.

The United States provided military assistance to India during the conflict, demonstrating that shared concerns over China could create space for cooperation.

The Difficult Phase: 1960s–1980s

Relations remained complicated because of Cold War geopolitics.

1971: India–Pakistan War

The 1971 India–Pakistan War became one of the lowest points in India–US relations. US supported Pakistan, while India had signed the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation.

The episode reinforced India's perception of the US as being strategically aligned with Pakistan.

1974: India's First Nuclear Test

India conducted its first nuclear test at Pokhran in 1974. US strongly opposed India's nuclear programme, and nuclear proliferation became a major source of tension.

Overall Character of the Cold War Period

India–US relations were shaped by:

• India's Non-Alignment
• US–Pakistan relations
• India–Soviet relations
• Nuclear differences
• Different approaches to Cold War politics

The relationship was therefore marked by strategic distance despite shared democratic values.

The Turning Point: 1991–2000

The end of the Cold War fundamentally changed the relationship. India also introduced economic liberalisation in 1991, creating new opportunities for trade, investment and technology cooperation. The collapse of the Soviet Union reduced the geopolitical importance of the earlier India–US divide.

1998: Nuclear Tests
India conducted nuclear tests at Pokhran in May 1998. The United States imposed sanctions, but diplomatic engagement continued.

1999: Kargil War

The Kargil War became an important turning point. The United States pressured Pakistan to withdraw its forces from the Line of Control.This contributed to greater strategic understanding between India and the US.

2000: Clinton's Visit

US President Bill Clinton's visit to India in 2000 marked a major improvement in bilateral relations.The relationship increasingly shifted from Cold War differences towards economic and strategic engagement.

Strategic Partnership: 2000–2008

The early 21st century witnessed a major transformation.

2005: Civil Nuclear Deal

The India–US Civil Nuclear Agreement became a landmark breakthrough.

It enabled greater civilian nuclear cooperation with India despite India not being a member of the NPT. The agreement eventually contributed to the 2008 NSG waiver, allowing India to participate in international civilian nuclear commerce.

Why It Was Important

• Reduced India's nuclear isolation.
• Opened civilian nuclear cooperation.
• Increased strategic trust.
• Recognised India's growing global importance.
• Fundamentally changed the bilateral relationship.

Defence Partnership: 2010s

Defence cooperation expanded rapidly.

The two countries increased:

• Military exercises
• Defence trade
• Maritime security cooperation
• Intelligence sharing
• Defence technology cooperation

India was designated a Major Defense Partner by the United States in 2016.

Major Defence Agreements

• LEMOA – 2016 Logistics support and access between the armed forces.

• COMCASA – 2018 Secure communications and interoperability.

• BECA – 2020 Sharing of geospatial information and advanced military data.

These agreements strengthened military cooperation while supporting India's defence modernisation.

Indo-Pacific: A New Strategic Pillar

The rise of China and growing strategic competition in the Indo-Pacific have created greater convergence between India and the United States.

The two countries cooperate through the Quad, along with Japan and Australia.

Areas of cooperation include:

• Maritime security
• Freedom of navigation
• Supply-chain resilience
• Critical technologies
• Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief
• A free, open and inclusive Indo-Pacific
The Indo-Pacific has therefore become one of the central pillars of contemporary India–US relations.

Technology & Emerging Sectors
The relationship has expanded beyond traditional defence and diplomacy.

Critical & Emerging Technology cooperation includes:

• Artificial Intelligence
• Semiconductors
• Quantum technology
• Biotechnology
• Telecommunications
• Cybersecurity

The Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) has strengthened cooperation in these areas.

Space

India and the US cooperate in:

• Earth observation
• Satellite technology
• Space exploration
• Human spaceflight
• Space situational awareness

Critical Minerals

Both countries are working towards resilient supply chains for minerals essential for:

• Electric vehicles
• Batteries
• Renewable energy
• Semiconductors
• Defence technology

Economic Relationship

The United States is one of India's most important economic partners.
Major areas include:
• Trade and investment
• Information technology
• Pharmaceuticals
• Electronics
• Defence manufacturing
• Energy
• Digital economy
• Services

The Indian diaspora in the United States also acts as an important bridge between the two countries.
Current Situation: 2025–26

The return of Donald Trump to the US presidency in January 2025 has introduced a more transactional dimension to the relationship.

Strategic cooperation remains strong, but trade, tariffs and India's relationship with Russia have emerged as major areas of friction.

Strategic Cooperation Continues

Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump met in February 2025 and reaffirmed the importance of the bilateral relationship.

The two sides focused on:

• Defence cooperation
• Trade and investment
• Critical and emerging technologies
• Critical minerals
• Energy security
• Space cooperation
• Indo-Pacific security

Thus, despite disagreements, the strategic foundation of the relationship remains strong.

Trade & Tariffs :
Trade has become one of the major areas of tension.
The Trump administration has pushed for:
• Lower Indian tariffs
• Greater market access for US goods
• Reduction of trade barriers
• A more balanced trade relationship

India and the US have continued negotiations towards a broader bilateral trade agreement.

The key challenge is balancing:

US demand for greater market access with India's protection of domestic producers and strategic sectors.

Russia: A Major Test

India's continued defence and energy relationship with Russia remains a sensitive issue. The United States has sought to pressure countries to reduce dependence on Russian energy.
India, however, continues to emphasise:
• Energy security
• Strategic autonomy
• National interest
• Independent foreign-policy decision-making
This creates a difficult balancing act for India.

India wants stronger ties with US without compromising its long-standing relationship with Russia.

Defence: Strongest Area of Convergence

Defence remains one of the strongest pillars of India–US relations.
Cooperation includes:
• Defence procurement
• Military exercises
• Maritime security
• Intelligence and surveillance
• Defence technology
• Co-production
• Indo-Pacific security

The relationship is increasingly moving from buyer–seller relations towards technology sharing and defence co-production.

China & the Indo-Pacific

China remains an important factor behind India–US strategic convergence.

Both countries seek:

• A free and open Indo-Pacific
• Secure sea lanes
• Resilient supply chains
• Greater maritime cooperation
• Reduced dependence on vulnerable supply chains

However, India does not want its relationship with the United States to become a formal anti-China alliance.

India's approach remains:
Strategic cooperation + Strategic autonomy

Why India–US Relations Are Strategically Important ?

1. Indo-Pacific Security
The US is an important partner in India's effort to maintain a free, open, inclusive and rules-based Indo-Pacific.

2. Defence Modernisation
US defence technology and cooperation can strengthen India's military capabilities and domestic defence manufacturing.

3. China

Growing Chinese influence has created greater strategic convergence between India and the US.

4. Technology

Cooperation in AI, semiconductors, quantum technology and space can strengthen India's technological capabilities.

5. Economic Security

Both countries have an interest in diversified and resilient supply chains.

6. Global Governance

India and the US increasingly cooperate on global challenges while India seeks a greater role in institutions such as the UN Security Council and other multilateral platforms.

India's Approach: Partnership Without Alliance

India's relationship with the US reflects its broader foreign-policy principle of strategic autonomy.
India cooperates closely with US on:
• Defence
• Technology
• Indo-Pacific security
• Counter-terrorism
• Critical minerals

At the same time, India maintains important relations with:
• Russia
• European countries
• Japan
• ASEAN
• West Asian countries

This reflects India's approach of multi-alignment — cooperating with different powers according to national interests rather than becoming part of a fixed alliance bloc.

India–US relations have travelled a long distance since 1947 from Cold War-era strategic distance to a comprehensive strategic partnership.The relationship today covers defence, technology, trade, space, critical minerals, energy and Indo-Pacific security. At the same time, differences over tariffs, trade, Russia and energy policy demonstrate that the partnership is not an alliance.

For India, the objective is to cooperate with the United States where interests converge, manage differences where they exist, and preserve strategic autonomy.

- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.

GoDaddy has challenged a Delhi High Court order that it says could reshape how the internet works far beyond India.

In December, the court blocked more than 1,100 fake websites impersonating brands like Amazon, McDonald's and Microsoft. But the ruling went further, issuing 14 directives that tech experts say rewrite the rules of internet governance. Domain sellers can no longer offer free privacy protection by default. A website owner's name, address, phone and email must be released to anyone with a "legitimate interest" within 72 hours. Domain names resembling protected brand names are prohibited outright.

GoDaddy, which manages 80 million domains for over 20 million customers, has filed a 5,121-page appeal arguing the order conflicts with India's own data protection law and the EU's GDPR. It warns the directives are commercially destabilising enough to force domain companies to exit India. Namecheap and Hosting Concepts have filed their own challenges.

India's concern is grounded in a real crisis. The government received 2.4 million cybercrime complaints last year involving losses of 2.4 billion dollars, and the Home Minister has said one person falls victim to cybercrime every 37 seconds. Court records show the directives closely followed submissions by the IT and home ministries.

Internet governance researchers warn the people exposed by public registration data will be journalists, activists and small business owners rather than fraudsters. GoDaddy points to a practical problem: protecting a trademark like HUL would overlap with 118 English words, including hulk and moghul.

A larger bench hears the appeals on July 16. A domestic anti-fraud ruling is quietly becoming a global internet governance precedent.

Source: Reuters

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

ANDROID

2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. The report says many of these orders were issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, which requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content to retain their legal protection. These are separate from blocking directions issued under Section 69A of the IT Act.

The report also says Meta has integrated its API with Sahyog to comply with the government’s 2–3-hour deadline, potentially allowing content flagged through government directions to be blocked automatically without a separate human review.

Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

How Modi Managed “THE MEDIA” To Stay In Power

In 2002, Gujarat CM Narendra Modi sat in front of a BBC camera and admitted his one real weakness:
“One area where I was very, very weak… that was how to handle the media.”

He never forgot that lesson. He just decided the media should never be allowed to become a problem again.
Fast forward to 2026.
Between March and July, the government sent one blocking order every 68 seconds to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube.

1.95 lakh orders in five months.
1,275 every single day.
Instagram — the platform students used during the Jantar Mantar protests — received more than 1 lakh of them.
Last year the daily average was six.

This is not “managing” the media.
This is industrial-scale silencing.

The same playbook that started with ED and CBI cases against NDTV, the takeover of Network18, and UAPA against NewsClick’s founder is now running on autopilot through the Sahyog portal. Content vanishes in three hours. Often without anyone even seeing the order.

A government that needs to issue a takedown every 68 seconds is not confident.
It is terrified of what people will say when they are not being watched.

That is how you stay in power for this long — not by answering questions, but by making sure the questions never reach the public.

When dissent is treated as a security threat and protest as a crime, the media is no longer a watchdog. It is just another department to be controlled.
The 2002 admission was honest.

The 2026 response is the real story. 68 seconds.
That’s how long this government takes to silence you.
He admitted one weakness in 2002. He spent the next 24 years making sure it never happened again.

text:
9 Critical Social Media and Platform Stories for Policy Watchers

Social media regulation, platform governance, and digital policy are moving fast across India and the globe. According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, here are 9 critical stories shaping the social media landscape today. This media monitoring roundup ensures you stay ahead of the curve.

1. [29.2026-08-21.190] Delhi HC Directs Centre to Consider Social Media Ban for Children
The Delhi High Court has declined to entertain a PIL seeking restrictions on social media access for children below 13, stating that such policy matters fall under the central government's domain. The court directed the government to consider the petition as a representation.
Why it matters: This case sets a precedent for how India approaches child online safety. The outcome could influence future legislation on social media use for minors.

Source: Hindustan Times, Free Press Journal, The Hans India, The Pioneer (4 sources)

2. [9.2026-08-21.94] Australia Imposes 2.5% Levy on Tech Giants for News Bargaining
Australia passed legislation imposing a 2.5% levy on advertising revenues of Meta and Google if they fail to strike commercial deals with local media outlets. This is a global first in supporting local news through tech regulation.
Why it matters: This could serve as a model for other countries, including India, seeking to compensate news publishers for content used on social platforms.

Source: Deccan Chronicle, Asian Age, Times of India (3 sources)

3. [9.2026-08-21.118] Meta Becomes One of Microsoft's Largest AI Customers
Meta is spending hundreds of millions of dollars annually to access AI models through Microsoft's Azure cloud service, using trillions of tokens per week. This highlights the growing demand for AI infrastructure within the tech industry.
Why it matters: The partnership underscores how social media giants are investing heavily in AI, reshaping the cloud and AI market.

Source: Business Standard, Deccan Chronicle, Asian Age (3 sources)

4. [28.2026-08-21.126] Meta Faces ₹14 Trillion Trial Over Targeting Children
Meta is being sued by a bipartisan coalition of U.S. states for allegedly designing addictive features that target children on Facebook and Instagram. The case seeks billions in damages and policy changes.
Why it matters: This case could fundamentally alter how social media platforms design features for younger users.

Source: Economic Times, Financial Express (2 sources)

5. [29.2026-08-21.102] Uttar Pradesh Restricts YouTuber Access to Government Schools
Basic education officers across multiple districts in UP have ordered that outsiders, including YouTubers, must seek prior permission for campus visits and video recording. This aims to ensure smooth teaching and learning.
Why it matters: This reflects growing concerns about social media influencers disrupting educational environments and privacy.

Source: Free Press Journal, Hindustan Times (2 sources)

6. [8.2026-08-21.233] Bihar Cabinet Approves Additional Payments for Social Media Creators
The Bihar cabinet amended the Bihar Social Media and Other Online Media Rules, 2026, allowing empanelled social media creators to earn extra payments for videos promoting state government schemes.
Why it matters: This incentivizes creators to produce government-related content, potentially setting a precedent for state-level influencer partnerships.

Source: Free Press Journal

7. [22.2026-08-21.114] Maharashtra Panel Suggests BNS Amendment for Defamatory Social Media Posts
A Maharashtra committee recommended amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita to cover defamatory social media posts, addressing an 11-year legal vacuum after the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A.
Why it matters: This could bring clarity to online defamation laws in India, balancing free speech with protection from misuse.

Source: Indian Express

8. [33.2026-08-21.104] Drishyam-Inspired Murders Raise Alarm Over Screen Violence
Psychologists warn that exposure to violent content in movies, online games, and social media videos is leading to copycat crimes, including the murder of a grandfather by four teenagers inspired by films.
Why it matters: This highlights the real-world consequences of unregulated violent content on social media platforms.

Source: New Indian Express

9. [28.2026-08-21.116] 80% of Indians Prefer Microdramas on Smartphones for Brand Engagement
A survey by Kantar, ShareChat & Moj reveals that 80% of Indians favor short-form video content on smartphones, with microdramas effectively boosting brand recognition and consumer trust.
Why it matters: This trend is reshaping digital marketing strategies, emphasizing the power of short-form content on social platforms.

Source: Financial Express

In conclusion, these stories underscore the dynamic intersection of social media, policy, and business. For a comprehensive press review of social media developments, Press Monitor delivers daily curated media intelligence from India's top print publications. Stay informed with print media monitoring that grounds your decisions in verified news.

In this edition of Press Monitor’s media monitoring roundup, we cover 9 critical stories on social media and platforms from Indian print media. Topics include the Delhi High Court’s directive on children’s social media use, Australia’s news bargaining levy on tech giants, Meta’s AI investment and trial, Uttar Pradesh restricting YouTubers in schools, Bihar incentivising social media creators, Maharashtra’s defamation law amendment, copycat crimes from screen violence, and the rise of microdramas for brand engagement. This media intelligence is powered by Press Monitor, delivering daily print media monitoring for policy watchers and industry professionals. Stay informed with Press Monitor.

About the Islamic Republic of Iran:  

Driven by extreme negative propaganda and the collaboration of leftist and communist groups—including those backed by the West—with Islamists, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi was overthrown in 1979 and left Iran on January 16; a key factor was his unwillingness to deploy the army—which remained loyal to him—more forcefully against his opponents among his own people.  

On February 1, 1979, the Islamist Ayatollah Khomeini, whom the Shah had sent into exile, returned to Iran. Within a short time, he established the Islamic Republic of Iran through brutal intimidation, electoral fraud, and repression. 
Supporters of the revolution from the leftist camp were quickly stripped of power and were among the first to be executed, alongside opponents of the regime who were loyal to the Shah or advocated for democracy. In total, up to 30,000 political prisoners were murdered in the years immediately following the revolution.  

Iraq’s invasion of Iran in 1980 triggered an eight-year war, in the shadow of which Islamic extremists were able to consolidate their power. Ali Khamenei, elected president in 1981 on Khomeini’s recommendation, stated in 1982: "The blessing of the war is unimaginably great for us." During the war, children were deployed as human "minesweepers," driven by the hundreds into minefields; they were promised that doing so would send them straight to paradise.  

Sharia

The Islamic regime introduced Sharia law. Since then, criticism of Islam—or even renouncing the faith—has been punishable by death. Other religions, such as the Baha'i faith, face suppression or even death threats. 

Women largely lost their rights; they are barred from holding high-ranking offices, cannot work or travel without the permission of their husbands or fathers, and are required to submit to male authority in all areas of life.  Under Article 301 of the Iranian Penal Code, for example, fathers and paternal grandfathers have the right to kill their children or grandchildren with impunity, as they are considered "blood of their blood." Women have only half the legal standing of men in court proceedings and inheritance matters. 

Child marriage for girls is permitted from the age of nine, although it is recommended only from the age of twelve. But state authorities actively promote child marriage; in 2021, approximately 70,000 children were born to mothers aged 15 to 19, and about 1,500 children were born to mothers under the age of 14.  

Husbands have the right to discipline their wives by beating them, engaging in sexual acts against their will, or raping them with impunity. 
If a woman commits adultery without being coerced, Article 630 of the Iranian Penal Code grants the husband the right to kill both her and her lover. 

A woman can only obtain a divorce if her husband fails to fulfill his sexual or financial obligations or subjects her to excessive corporal punishment without valid reason. A man, conversely, need only declare the divorce before three male witnesses for it to become legally binding—even without the woman’s knowledge. 
It was only after years of protests by women that, as of 2013, they gained the right to petition the courts for divorce; however, women must prove the aforementioned grounds for divorce in court. 

Severe penalties await women who fail to comply with the headscarf mandate; homosexuality is punishable by death—for instance, through public stoning or hanging. Western music and films, as well as men and women dancing or singing together—and, of course, alcohol—are strictly prohibited and severely punished.  

Compliance with these regulations is enforced by the religious police and the Revolutionary Guards. Political opponents and those who violate strict religious laws face show trials, imprisonment, and even public flogging, torture, mutilation, stoning (in cases of adultery), and public executions.  

Terror Regime

The mullahs base their power on the Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)—designated as a terrorist organization by many countries—and the Basij militia, which together comprise approximately one million fighters. 

Units of the IRGC also operate abroad; through them, the Islamic regime supports terrorist organizations worldwide—such as Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Houthis in Yemen, and Islamic Jihad—orchestrates terrorist attacks, controls vast areas of Iraq and Lebanon via brutal Shiite militias, props up the Assad regime, and has regime opponents assassinated abroad.  

The destruction of Israel is an official state objective of the brutal mullah regime. A public clock counts down to the total annihilation of Israel and all Jews by the year 2040 at the latest. The regime has at times paid bounties for the killing of Jews abroad and supported the Hamas massacre of Jews on October 7, 2023, in which over 1,000 people were murdered.  

Despite international treaties, Iran is working on a nuclear bomb—which would render it invulnerable—and already possesses approximately 400 kg of highly enriched (60%) uranium, enough for about nine bombs. An enrichment level of only about 5% is entirely sufficient for the peaceful use of nuclear energy. 
With a range of up to 4,000 km, Iran's missiles can now reach cities such as Berlin, Paris, Rome, or London, thereby posing a concrete threat to Europe.  

Following rigged elections that favored the ultra-conservative Mahmoud Ahmadinejad over the somewhat more liberal Mir Hossein Mousavi, a nationwide wave of protests—known as the "Green Revolution"—erupted in 2009. The girl "Neda", who was killed during these events, became a symbol of the freedom movement.  
Over the years, further mass demonstrations and smaller uprisings occurred repeatedly (2017/18, 2019), each of which was brutally suppressed. In the aftermath, thousands of regime opponents were executed—a figure that, relative to population size, exceeds that of any other country in the world.  

During the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement following the murder of Jina Mahsa Amini in 2022–23, thousands of people—predominantly young—were once again killed by the regime; thousands more were blinded or maimed by targeted shotgun fire or executed in the years that followed. As a deterrent, hundreds of schoolchildren who had taken part in protests were also poisoned.  
In 2025 alone, at least 2,159 people were executed in Iran—accounting for approximately 80% of documented cases worldwide. The fates of thousands of others remain unknown.  

The economic situation in Iran is catastrophic. The country suffers not primarly from Western sanctions but, above all, from the mismanagement and corruption of the ruling apparatus itself. 
The Revolutionary Guards control vast sectors of the economy, particularly the oil industry. Revenues are invested almost exclusively in weapons systems, the nuclear program, and the sponsorship of terrorism; the remainder lines the pockets of corrupt regime members. To survive amidst extreme inflation, ordinary people are forced to hold multiple jobs—usually at least two—often resulting in actual working hours exceeding 16 hours a day. 
Despite this, large segments of the population are sinking further into poverty.  This situation—compounded by the hopelessness and depression caused by the political system—has led to a massive surge in drug use, even though drug trafficking and possession carry severe penalties, including the death penalty. 
Many women, particularly widows and orphans, are left without means of support for themselves and their children and are forced into prostitution to survive. This practice is often tacitly facilitated by mullahs through short-term marriages (*sigheh*), yet simultaneously prosecuted and punished by the morality police.  Illegal organ trafficking—or the sale of one’s own organs in order to survive—is also becoming an increasing problem.  

Beginning in the autumn of 2025, nationwide peaceful protests erupted once more, with repeated calls for the overthrow of Ayatollah Khamenei and an end to the regime. Slogans such as "Javid Shah" (Long live the King) and "This is the final battle—Pahlavi returns" demanded the return of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi. The rallying cry frequently heard—"Down with the three corrupt ones"—refers to the collaboration between mullahs, leftists, and the Mujahedin to overthrow the Shah. 
The protests reached their interim peak in January 2026. 

On January 8 and 9, a brutal massacre of demonstrators was perpetrated by the IRGC and the Basij. Within just two days, approximately 50,000 people (with some estimates reaching up to 100,000) were savagely murdered by the regime—in some cases with machine guns—and hundreds of thousands were injured.  
The regime even had doctors and nurses killed as they attempted to treat wounded protesters; the injured themselves were mercilessly slaughtered. 
To prevent images of the protests and atrocities from reaching the outside world, the regime subsequently blocked the population's access to the internet and telephone networks for approximately three months.  

Setting aside all theoretical considerations regarding international law, the war waged by the USA and Israel against the Islamic Republic of Iran is welcomed by the vast majority of the Iranian people, who view it as a rescue mission for the population. 
During the first week of the war, large segments of the population cheered every bomb that struck the regime. News of Ayatollah Khamenei’s death, in particular, sparked great jubilation. 
By now, however, the regime’s IRGC terrorists are firing from the street at any open window from which music or cheering can be heard, thereby stifling the celebration in bloodshed.  

Since the start of the war, the regime has had its back against the wall; its leaders—senior mullahs, IRGC commanders, and the like—have hidden in bunkers during attacks, often beneath schools and kindergartens, to avoid being targeted by bombs. 
Dramatic internal power struggles have ensued, yet repression and executions continue unabated.  

Since the beginning of the year, hundreds of innocent young people have been tortured and then hanged from construction cranes in this manner, with further executions taking place daily. 
Scarcely a day goes by without the execution of several young people who participated in the protests. Young women who are still virgins are raped before being murdered, as Islamic law holds that virgins would otherwise go straight to heaven.
The bodies of the victims are often desecrated, and their hair or organs are frequently sold. 
To bury their murdered children, brothers, and sisters, relatives are forced to sign statements claiming the victims were killed by demonstrators or were Israeli agents; they often have to pay large sums of money to secure the release of the bodies.  

Because elements of the army, the IRGC, and the Basij have been severely weakened by the attacks—and some are reportedly no longer willing to fire upon their own people—the regime increasingly relies on particularly brutal Iraqi and Afghan mercenary groups.

Contrary to the regime's propaganda, there are few civilian casualties resulting from the war itself. 

According to all reports, the vast majority of the Iranian population would rather endure the consequences of war for a longer period than continue suffering under the oppression and terror of the mullah regime, the IRGC, and the Basij; consequently, they welcome further attacks on the regime. Global Embarrassment

The government’s clumsy and ridiculous manner of “implementing” the Supreme Court’s order regarding Imran Khan’s health has brought disgrace and humiliation upon this government internationally.

The Supreme Court’s clear order was that Imran Khan should be taken to Shifa Hospital, where a medical board comprising Shifa’s doctors, in the presence of Imran’s personal physician and his sister, Dr. Uzma, would examine him, and that he would remain ostensibly there until September 16, when the court was to review the entire record.

At 12:23, Imran Khan was taken to PIMS Hospital, and at 5:00 he was declared healthy and sent back to jail.

This clearly demonstrates that the Shehbaz government was unwilling to comply with the Supreme Court’s order. Playing fast and loose with the law has long been the PML-N’s modus operandi—whether it was removing Junejo from the party presidency and creating the PML-N, the Memogate case, the attack on the judiciary, Nawaz Sharif’s platelet case, or the case of Imran Khan.

Had the government honestly implemented the Supreme Court’s decision, it would have deserved appreciation, political pressure would have eased, and an environment conducive to dialogue with the PTI would have emerged. But the PML-N leadership, blinded by its hatred for Imran Khan, appears determined to settle old scores.

Now condemnation is raining down from around the world.

And political tensions in the country will intensify further. So, whose bed will be rolled up next? Let us see. How long will the Field Marshal tolerate the stench of the hybrid system, when his office (CDSO) has, through an emergency amendment, been made autonomous from and superior to the Ministry of Defence, with sweeping powers?

It seems the Sharif Company has lost its bearings. It does not want PTI to settle its differences with the military. Yet Zulfi Bukhari, one of Imran Khan’s closest associates, welcomed the Supreme Court’s decision and had assured that there would be peaceful coexistence with the establishment.

Now the question is whether the Supreme Court will stand firm over its contempt, or whether the Shehbaz government will quietly retreat with its tail between its legs.

And if the PPP joins the Grand Opposition after the inclusion of Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who will save the PML-N’s lights from being extinguished, when the CDS office has become autonomous and beyond the Ministry of Defence, while the unemployed Defence Minister, Khawaja Asif, shamelessly sits outside the ministry’s door, crying over the same old grievances?

By Imtiaz Alam

Under South African law, a coordinated group (“mob”) attacking, harassing, or belittling a person on X can trigger both criminal and civil liability. The consequences depend on the exact conduct (threats, insults, doxxing, repeated messages, coordinated pile-ons, etc.), but several statutes apply directly.

Criminal offences
Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020**  
  Section 14: Unlawfully and intentionally disclosing or threatening to disclose a data message that is harmful (includes messages that cause mental, psychological, physical or economic harm). A coordinated group campaign can easily meet this threshold. 

  Section 15: Cyber harassment / cyberbullying – repeatedly sending data messages that cause the target fear, anxiety, humiliation, or distress.  
  Section 16: Incitement of violence or harm via data messages.  
  Penalties: fines and/or imprisonment (up to 5–10 years depending on the section and aggravating factors). Police can investigate on a complaint; the NPA can prosecute.

Protection from Harassment Act 17 of 2011**  
  Applies to electronic communications. A protection order can be obtained in the Magistrate’s Court; breach of the order is a criminal offence (fine or imprisonment up to 5 years). Courts have granted such orders against online pile-ons.

Intimidation Act 72 of 1982 / common-law intimidation**  
  If the posts contain threats of violence, damage to property, or other harm, this can be charged as intimidation.

Criminal defamation* (still recognised, though rarely used) and *crimen iniuria** (impairment of dignity). Serious public belittling or humiliation can lead to charges, especially when done by a group.

Civil remedies
Defamation** (common-law): The target can sue the individuals (and sometimes platforms in limited circumstances) for damages. South African courts have awarded substantial damages for social-media defamation, and a group campaign increases the quantum because of the wider publication and malice.  
Actio iniuriarum** (injury to personality/dignity).  
Interdicts (injunctions) to stop the posts and compel removal. Courts can order X to take down content and identify anonymous posters via subpoena.

Additional possible liability
Hate speech** under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) if the content targets a protected ground (race, gender, religion, etc.). Equality Court can order apologies, damages, and publication of findings.  
If the mob involves doxxing or encouraging real-world harm, further charges under the Cybercrimes Act or common-law assault/intimidation become available.

Practical notes
South African police (SAPS Cybercrime units) and the National Prosecuting Authority do investigate social-media harassment cases, especially when a formal complaint is laid with evidence (screenshots, handles, timestamps).  
Anonymous accounts can still be pursued: courts can order X (or the ISP) to disclose user data under the Cybercrimes Act and the Regulation of Interception of Communications Act.  
Group organisers or those who actively recruit others face higher risk of being treated as principal offenders or accessories.  
Free-speech defences exist (truth, fair comment, public interest), but coordinated personal attacks and insults rarely qualify.

In short: a deliberate group campaign to attack or belittle someone on X is not “just free speech.” It can result in criminal charges under the Cybercrimes Act and Protection from Harassment Act, protection orders, civil damages for defamation or dignity infringement, and possible Equality Court proceedings. Victims are advised to preserve evidence and consult a lawyer or lay a complaint with SAPS.

PUBLIC LEGAL NOTICE

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:
1. THE UNIDENTIFIED INDIVIDUAL (JANE DOE) 
Featured in Subject Instagram Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)

2. THE GRIEVANCE OFFICER & LEGAL CELL
  Meta Platforms, Inc. / Instagram LLC
  (Intermediary hosting subject digital broadcast)

3. TO WHOMSOEVER IT MAY CONCERN / GENERAL PUBLIC
SUBJECT: LEGAL NOTICE DEMANDING CEASE & DESIST, IMMEDIATE TAKEDOWN OF UNLAWFUL DIGITAL CONTENT, PUBLIC RETRACTION, AND INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS), 2023 AND THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

B. TAKEDOWN AND DELETION - Ensure the immediate deletion and permanent takedown of the impugned Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)from Instagram and all mirror platforms.

C. PUBLIC APOLOGY / RETRACTION- Issue an unconditional public apology across official digital channels acknowledging the improper nature of the broadcast and expressing regret.
 
TAKE NOTICE that if you fail to strictly comply with the terms of this Legal Notice within the stipulated period of 7 (Seven) days, it shall be constrained to initiate appropriate civil and criminal proceedings against you—including filing a formal First Information Report (FIR) under the relevant provisions of BNS, 2023 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000, alongside seeking direction from the competent Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) of BNSS, 2023—entirely at your risk, cost, and legal consequences.
 
A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit
Advocate
Rajasthan High Court

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Special thanks to Sr. Adv. Makarand D. Adkar Ji (@AdkarMakarand) for his guidance and support, and to the legal team for their efforts.

@OpIndia @TheBharatPost @TimesNow @SanatanPrabhat @MeghUpdates

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India Orders Immediate Takedown of Dhruv Rathee’s (@dhruv_rathee)  Video.

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, Government of India, has passed an Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) directing YouTube to remove the video titled “Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed” within 24 hours of receiving the Order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it has been uploaded today (19 July 2026).

Key points from the GAC Order:

- The video contains deliberate and malicious statements insulting Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.

- It falsely claims they consumed meat (including deer meat) and alcohol, using distorted references from scriptures.

- Such content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is against societal harmony.

UPDATE TO ALL MEMBERS ON LOCUM ENGAGEMENT & CASUALIZATION

The leadership of NARD, ably led by the Strategic P-MUS (Garkuwan Matasan Arewa), is pleased to update members on the outcome of the FMoHSW Committee on  Regulation and Casualization of Doctors.

Following extensive consultations, the Committee has developed a National Policy on the Engagement of Locum, aimed at ensuring fair, transparent and non-exploitative engagement of temporary healthcare personnel.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recruitment & Approval:
   Locum engagement must be based on a clearly identified staffing gap and approved by the appropriate hospital authorities.

2. Contract Duration:
   Initial locum contracts shall not exceed 6 months, with only one additional 6-month renewal permitted. Continuous engagement for 12 months makes the position eligible for permanent appointment.

3. Maximum Work Hours:
   Healthcare personnel shall work a maximum of 48 hours per week, including weekends. Excess hours must be appropriately compensated.

4. Maximum Duty Period:
   No healthcare personnel shall work beyond 24 continuous hours, including call duty.

5. Mandatory Rest:
   
   - Minimum 12 hours between shifts.

   - Mandatory 24-hour post-call rest after weekday and weekend calls.

   - A 1-hour break after 6 hours of continuous work.

6. Call Duty:
   
   - Maximum 2 calls per week.

   - Maximum 1 weekend call per month.

   - Calls must be equitably distributed.

7. Remuneration & Welfare:
Pay rates are standardized in alignment with the government's 
Scheme of Service. Remuneration must be paid monthly without delay, accompanied by monthly 
payslips. 

Locum staff are entitled to all government-approved leaves, public holidays, and occupational insurance coverage.

8. Excess Work Hours:
   Excess hours must be properly documented, monitored and adequately compensated, or appropriately balanced with structured time-off.

9. Protection Against Abuse:
   Locum engagement must not be used as a permanent substitute for substantive recruitment or as a means of exploiting healthcare workers.

10. Integration & Safety: All locum workers must undergo mandatory orientation and integration into their respective clinical or administrative teams. Institutions are required to provide safe 
working environment, adequate call rooms, refreshments during prolonged calls/shifts, and burnout prevention programs.

11. Discipline & Grievance Process: Professional misconduct shall be governed by the regulatory 
council guidelines. Contracts can be terminated by either party with a one-month notice or payment in lieu, and all accrued entitlements must be settled within 14 days of termination. Disputes escalate through institutional mechanisms up to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment.

12. Monitoring: The Ministry would ensure Institutions do not engage in exploitative staffing practices and violations of this guideline in line with the Nigerian Labour Law.

13. Policy Review and Effective Date:
This policy becomes legally binding on the exact date of approval by the Federal Ministry of 
Health and Social Welfare (FMoH&SW). To ensure its continuous operational relevance, the 
policy mandates a comprehensive evaluation and review within two (2) years of its 
implementation.

The policy is expected to provide a more structured and equitable framework for locum engagement across Nigerian health institutions.

text: Although every schoolchild learns (or is supposed to learn) that the President is the Chief Executive, our country went through a period a few decades ago when Congress routinely insulated certain Executive officials from Executive control. So it was with the Foreign Service; a 1980 law created a Grievance Board to which Foreign Service officers can appeal certain adverse disciplinary actions, including termination. The Secretary of State appoints the Board’s members for fixed terms (which can outlast the Secretary’s own tenure) but neither the Secretary nor even the President can remove those members except for cause. And that Board, not the Secretary or the President, is given the final say in the Executive Branch on many disciplinary matters—the Board effectively has the power to overrule the Secretary and the President on whether particular conduct—e.g. alcoholism, drug use, spousal abuse, or even espionage—warrants disciplinary consequences and, if so, what kind. I’m pleased that @TheJusticeDept has recognized that the law creating the Grievance Board is to that extent unconstitutional. Under our Constitution, the President and the Secretary of State must have the final word on whether Foreign Service officers, who represent our country abroad, are subject to disciplinary consequences, including termination, for their actions.

🚨 TAX / LEGAL ALERT: A “Fit-Out Possession” Is Not Legal Possession; Builder Remains Liable for Delay Until Complete and Lawful Possession Is Delivered

🔹 What Happened: The Assessee had booked a residential unit and paid substantial consideration. The Agreement for Sale dated 04.10.2019 stipulated possession by 31.07.2021. The Department/opposite parties later issued a letter dated 11.11.2024 offering only “fit-out possession”, subject to payment of the balance consideration and completion of further formalities. An Occupation Certificate was subsequently produced, but the Completion Certificate was not brought on record.

🔍 Key Takeaways:

• Possession/Documentation: “Fit-out possession” or paper possession does not amount to actual, complete and lawful possession. Valid possession requires the unit to be complete, habitable and legally capable of occupation, including compliance with the requisite completion formalities.

• Completion Certificate: An Occupation Certificate and Completion Certificate are distinct documents. Mere issuance of an Occupation Certificate does not cure the absence of a Completion Certificate where the latter is required for lawful possession.

• Financial Liability: The COVID-19 period granted the Assessee only the recognised 9-month extension. Since possession was not validly delivered even by 30.04.2022, the Department remained liable for continuing delay. Compensation was therefore directed at 9% p.a. on the amount deposited, from 30.04.2022 until actual complete possession.

• Settlement/Release: A settlement executed when the builder retained possession and had substantially greater bargaining power could not defeat the Assessee’s statutory consumer remedy where the settlement appeared to have been procured under economic compulsion and unequal bargaining power. The fact that the agreed Rs.5 lakh compensation had also not been paid further weakened the Department’s reliance on the settlement.

• Final Relief: The complaint was partly allowed with costs. The Department was directed to deliver complete and habitable possession after obtaining a valid and final Completion Certificate within 3 months, without penalty/delayed interest; pay 9% p.a. delay compensation, Rs.75,000 for mental agony/harassment and Rs.35,000 litigation costs, subject to the further interest consequences specified in the order.
